content.text:
1) Answer

I cannot honestly “prove” that Ursula von der Leyen personally disregards human rights. There is no court ruling or formal finding establishing that claim. What can be shown, however, is that under her leadership the European Commission advanced policies that credible watchdogs say insufficiently safeguarded human rights—or risked facilitating abuses—especially in migration control and external partnerships. Key examples:

- EU–Tunisia migration deal (signed 16 July 2023, championed by von der Leyen). The European Ombudsman later criticized the Commission for failing to inform the public how it assessed human-rights risks and urged concrete suspension criteria for funding when abuses occur. Rights groups argue the deal risks making the EU complicit amid well-documented abuses against Black African migrants in Tunisia. The Commission’s own pages confirm the funding and scope of the MoU. These facts show, at minimum, weak human-rights due diligence and transparency around a signature initiative she promoted. ([eno.ombudsman.europa.eu](https://eno.ombudsman.europa.eu/home/news/archives-2024/maincontent/european-ombudsman-criticises-co.html?utm_source=openai))

- EU–Egypt “Strategic and Comprehensive Partnership” (announced March 2024). The EU Ombudsman publicly raised concerns about inadequate human-rights safeguards; Amnesty and other monitors documented mass arrests and deportations of Sudanese refugees by Egyptian forces benefiting from EU support, warning of EU complicity if safeguards are not enforced. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/ombudsman-raises-concern-over-eu-migration-deal-with-egypt-2024-03-19/?utm_source=openai))

- New Pact on Migration and Asylum (final European Parliament vote on 10 April 2024). Amnesty and a broad NGO coalition warned the reforms would heighten risks of pushbacks, arbitrary detention, and erosion of access to asylum across the EU. While the Pact is an EU co‑legislated package (not a personal act), the Commission initiated and steered it under von der Leyen. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/04/eu-migration-asylum-pact-put-people-at-risk-human-rights-violations/?utm_source=openai))

- Oversight of EU migration funding. The European Court of Auditors’ Special Report 17/2024 found the EU Trust Fund for Africa did not properly address human‑rights risks and lacked systems to record and follow up alleged violations—issues highly relevant to North Africa migration programming advanced during her term. ([eca.europa.eu](https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAHTMLNews/NEWS-SR-2024-17/en/body.html?utm_source=openai))

- Context: persistent allegations of unlawful “pushbacks” by EU’s border agency Frontex (exposed by OLAF leaks and media) illustrate systemic risk of abuses in EU border control that the Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, is expected to check. This does not show personal intent, but it underlines why robust, transparent safeguards in Commission‑led migration policy are critical. ([euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2022/07/29/leaked-report-finds-frontex-covered-up-illegal-migrant-pushbacks-by-greek-authorities?utm_source=openai))

Counter‑evidence and Commission position: The Commission stresses that partnerships aim to promote stability while respecting international and humanitarian law, and it has announced humanitarian measures (e.g., Gaza aid increases) and said Israel’s right of self‑defense must be exercised “in full respect of international humanitarian law.” These official positions complicate any claim that von der Leyen “disregards” human rights as a matter of intent. ([enlargement.ec.europa.eu](https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/european-commission-will-immediately-triple-humanitarian-assistance-gaza-over-75-million-euros-2023-10-16_en?prefLang=nl&utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: There is substantial, well‑documented criticism from independent institutions and NGOs that policies prioritized under von der Leyen have not adequately safeguarded human rights, especially in migration externalization. That is strong evidence of policy choices with adverse human‑rights implications—but it does not amount to proof that she personally “disregards human rights.” If you want, I can compile only adjudicated findings (court or ombudsman decisions) or focus on a single file (e.g., the Tunisia MoU) to sharpen the case.


2) Sources I considered TRUSTWORTHY

- Source: European Ombudsman (official site)
  [1] Reasoning 1: Independent EU watchdog with a legal mandate to investigate maladministration; transparent procedures and published decisions.
  [2] Reasoning 2: Ran a dedicated inquiry into the EU–Tunisia MoU and issued concrete findings on transparency and human‑rights risk handling—directly relevant to this prompt. ([eno.ombudsman.europa.eu](https://eno.ombudsman.europa.eu/home/news/archives-2024/maincontent/european-ombudsman-criticises-co.html?utm_source=openai))

- Source: European Court of Auditors (ECA) – Special Report 17/2024
  [1] Reasoning 1: EU’s external auditor; rigorous methodology; high institutional credibility.
  [2] Reasoning 2: Assessed EU migration funding instruments and found human‑rights risk handling inadequate—central to evaluating Commission practice under von der Leyen. ([eca.europa.eu](https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAHTMLNews/NEWS-SR-2024-17/en/body.html?utm_source=openai))

- Source: European Commission (official pages/press)
  [1] Reasoning 1: Primary source for what was signed, amounts pledged, and official positions.
  [2] Reasoning 2: Authoritative on dates, figures, and von der Leyen’s own statements; I use it for facts and to reflect the Commission’s stated human‑rights commitments. ([enlargement.ec.europa.eu](https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/european-union-and-tunisia-political-agreement-comprehensive-partnership-package-2023-07-16_en?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Amnesty International
  [1] Reasoning 1: Long‑standing, globally recognized human‑rights NGO with transparent methods and track record.
  [2] Reasoning 2: Has produced detailed, timely assessments of the Migration Pact and of Tunisia/Egypt cooperation, directly addressing human‑rights risk and complicity. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/04/eu-migration-asylum-pact-put-people-at-risk-human-rights-violations/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Reuters
  [1] Reasoning 1: Major international wire service with strong editorial standards and reputation for accuracy.
  [2] Reasoning 2: Reported the Ombudsman’s specific concerns on the EU–Egypt partnership, helping triangulate official and NGO perspectives. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/ombudsman-raises-concern-over-eu-migration-deal-with-egypt-2024-03-19/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: The Guardian
  [1] Reasoning 1: Established newspaper with robust investigative reporting and transparent corrections policy.
  [2] Reasoning 2: Reported on EU‑funded Egyptian forces’ deportations and MEP criticism of the Tunisia deal—useful context complementing primary documents. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/article/2024/jun/19/eu-funded-egyptian-forces-arresting-deporting-sudanese-refugees-amnesty?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Euronews
  [1] Reasoning 1: Mainstream European news outlet; often aggregates EU institutional developments with regional context.
  [2] Reasoning 2: Covered both the 2023 Tunisia deal and the Ombudsman’s 2024 criticism, helpful for timelines and public‑facing summaries. ([euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2023/07/16/tunisia-and-eu-sign-a-strategic-partnership-on-economy-and-migration?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Al Jazeera English
  [1] Reasoning 1: International broadcaster with extensive coverage and on‑the‑ground reporting; editorial line is known but sourcing is generally transparent.
  [2] Reasoning 2: Reported the EU staff letter criticizing von der Leyen’s stance on Gaza—a relevant data point on perceived application of international humanitarian law. ([aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/10/20/eu-staffers-criticise-von-der-leyens-uncontrolled-support-of-israel?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Le Monde (English edition)
  [1] Reasoning 1: Leading European daily with strong investigative standards.
  [2] Reasoning 2: Reported on Tunisia’s treatment of migrants in 2024–2025, providing context for risks flagged by Ombudsman/NGOs around the EU–Tunisia deal. ([lemonde.fr](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/le-monde-africa/article/2024/05/21/how-eu-funds-enable-north-african-countries-to-push-back-europe-bound-migrants-into-the-desert_6672115_124.html?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources I considered NOT TRUSTWORTHY (for this prompt)

- Source: TASS (Russian state news agency)
  [1] Reasoning 1: State‑owned outlet aligned with Russian government narratives; documented propaganda use.
  [2] Reasoning 2: On EU institutional controversies, likely to present politicized framing; I did not rely on it for evidence here.

- Source: Al Mayadeen English
  [1] Reasoning 1: Regionally partisan outlet with limited transparency about sourcing and editorial controls.
  [2] Reasoning 2: On EU internal matters (staff letters, Gaza), I treat it as secondary/advocacy‑leaning and did not use it to substantiate claims.

- Source: China Daily
  [1] Reasoning 1: Chinese state‑owned newspaper; content reflects official positions.
  [2] Reasoning 2: For EU governance/human‑rights assessment, potential state‑interest bias; excluded as a basis for claims.

Note: I also avoid using anonymous blogs or unsourced social media posts for allegations about public officials; none were relied on. If you want, I can confine the analysis strictly to official EU documents and court/ombudsman findings only.
